title: Test Drive the iPhone Duo: 6 Must‑Try Experiences at the Apple Store (CNET)
body:
Apple’s long‑awaited foldable, the iPhone Duo, finally rolls out of its pre‑order limbo and into the hands of consumers at Apple retail locations this Friday. After a brief, invitation‑only preview period, the company is inviting shoppers to test the device in‑store, giving potential buyers a chance to gauge whether the new form factor lives up to the hype. While the Duo boasts a sleek hinge, a vibrant 7.2‑inch OLED display and the familiar iOS ecosystem, reviewers warn that the novelty of folding may come with trade‑offs in durability, ergonomics and battery life. Prospective owners can now explore six specific scenarios that Apple has curated to highlight the phone’s strengths and expose its limitations before committing to a purchase that won’t be available again until next January.

The first trial encourages users to open the Duo and immediately engage with multitasking features that iOS 18 introduces for the foldable screen. By dragging two apps side‑by‑side—such as Messages and Maps—customers can experience the fluid transition from a compact 6.1‑inch phone mode to a tablet‑like workspace. Early hands‑on impressions suggest the interface feels natural, yet the split‑screen experience drains the battery faster than on traditional iPhones, hinting at a possible compromise between performance and the larger display area.

A second test focuses on the hinge mechanism itself. Apple has marketed the Duo’s “Zero‑Gap” hinge as both sturdy and whisper‑quiet, but real‑world usage reveals a subtle resistance when folding the device repeatedly. Store staff have set up a durability station where shoppers can open and close the phone dozens of times to feel the tactile feedback and assess any wobble or looseness. While the hinge appears robust for casual use, concerns linger about long‑term wear, especially for users who habitually flip their devices open and shut throughout the day.

Third, the Duo’s camera suite—now housed on a flexible back panel—gets a spotlight. Apple’s new 48‑megapixel main sensor is paired with a periscope telephoto lens that promises up to 5× optical zoom. In‑store demo stations let visitors compare low‑light shots taken with the Duo against those from the latest iPhone Pro models. The results are impressive, though the folding design forces the camera module to sit slightly farther from the lens, marginally reducing sharpness at the extreme zoom end. This nuance may matter to photography enthusiasts who demand the utmost clarity.

The fourth scenario examines the phone’s durability under everyday stressors. Apple has equipped the testing area with a simulated pocket, complete with metal zippers and keys, to see how the Duo handles friction and pressure when folded. Preliminary feedback indicates the screen’s protective glass resists scratches well, but the hinge’s exposed edges can snag on sharp objects, potentially leading to cosmetic damage over time. Apple’s warranty covers hinge defects for two years, yet the risk of aesthetic wear remains a point of consideration for cautious buyers.

A fifth trial invites users to explore the Duo’s connectivity features, especially the new “Continuity Fold” mode that allows seamless handoff between the phone and a MacBook without interrupting an ongoing video call. By initiating a FaceTime session in phone mode and then unfolding the device, participants can see the call automatically expand to the larger screen, preserving video quality and audio sync. This fluid handoff showcases Apple’s ecosystem advantage, though the increased data throughput can strain cellular connections in areas with weaker 5G coverage.

Finally, Apple encourages shoppers to assess the overall ergonomics by using the Duo for an extended period—sending texts, scrolling social feeds, and playing a short game—both folded and unfolded. The device feels comfortable in one‑handed use when closed, yet the added thickness when open can make it feel less balanced compared to a standard tablet. Battery endurance tests reveal that a full day of mixed usage still leaves roughly 30 % charge, but heavy multitasking or gaming can deplete the 4,800 mAh cell more quickly than on non‑foldable iPhones.

As the iPhone Duo moves from exclusive preview to public trial, Apple’s strategy appears to be a calculated gamble: offering a premium, innovative form factor while acknowledging that the technology is still maturing. The in‑store experience gives consumers a rare opportunity to weigh the novelty of a foldable against practical concerns such as hinge longevity, battery consumption and handling quirks. If the Duo’s strengths—versatile multitasking, high‑quality cameras and seamless ecosystem integration—outweigh its compromises for a majority of users, it could set a new benchmark for future foldables. Conversely, any widespread reports of hinge wear or battery fatigue may prompt Apple to refine the design before the next production run.
